mercy_translation.text:
Who among all human beings who ever lived formed for himself a body from a virgin alone? Or what human being ever healed such diseases as the common Lord of all? Who restored what was lacking from birth and made a person blind from birth able to see?

Asclepius was deified among them because he practiced medicine and devised herbs for bodily illnesses—not creating the herbs from the earth himself, but discovering them through knowledge of nature. But what is this compared with what the Savior accomplished? He did not merely heal a wound; he fashioned what was lacking from birth and restored the creature.

Heracles is worshiped as a god among the Greeks because he fought against human beings equal to himself and killed wild beasts by cleverness. What is this compared with the works of the Word, who drove diseases, demons, and death itself away from human beings? Dionysus is worshiped among them because he became a teacher of drunkenness to human beings. But the true Savior and Lord of the universe, who taught self-control, is mocked by them.

But let these things be. What will they say about the other wonders of his divinity? At whose death among human beings was the sun darkened and the earth shaken? Look: human beings still die now and have died before. When did such a wonder happen at their deaths?

Or, leaving aside the deeds performed through his body, let us recall what has taken place since his resurrection. Whose teaching among all human beings who ever lived has prevailed as one and the same from one end of the earth to the other, so that reverence for him has flown throughout the whole earth?

And if, according to them, Christ is a human being and not God the Word, why is reverence for him not prevented by the gods among them from entering the very regions where they are worshiped? Instead, the Word himself, by coming there, brings their worship to an end through his teaching and puts their illusion to shame.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius compares Christ with deified figures of Greek religion as part of his apologetic.
The argument from the worldwide spread of Christian teaching reflects Athanasius' fourth-century perspective.
